title: West Virginia v. Environmental Protection Agency (2022)
shortTitle: West Virginia v. Environmental Protection Agency (2022)
summary: EPA lacked clear congressional authorization for the Clean Power Plan’s generation-shifting system. The competing opinions disagreed about the meaning of a broad delegation and the legitimacy of a distinct major-questions clear-authorization requirement.
notes: Roberts wrote for a 6-3 Court; Gorsuch concurred (joined by Alito) setting out a framework for the major questions doctrine; Kagan dissented, joined by Breyer and Sotomayor.

sections.Parties: West Virginia, other states, and coal-industry parties sought review of the D.C. Circuit’s judgment rejecting EPA’s repeal of the Clean Power Plan. EPA and parties supporting its authority defended the broader construction of the Clean Air Act. The dispute concerned EPA’s legal authority to choose the method for limiting existing power plants’ carbon emissions; the Court did not decide climate science or prescribe a preferred energy policy. (Printed 967–975.)
sections.Material Facts:
Clean Air Act § 111 required performance standards reflecting the emission reduction achievable through the best adequately demonstrated system, considering statutory factors including costs, other environmental effects, and energy requirements. For existing plants under § 111(d), EPA determined the needed reduction and states implemented source-level limits. Earlier uses principally improved the emissions performance of regulated sources through technology or operating practices. (Printed 967–969.)

EPA’s 2015 Clean Power Plan used three building blocks. More efficient coal-plant operation supplied the first. The other two shifted electricity generation from coal to gas and from fossil fuels to renewables. Operators could reduce their own production, build or subsidize cleaner generation, or purchase credits. EPA modeled the feasible shift and set limits that existing coal plants could not meet solely by changing their own equipment or operation. The projected transition reduced coal’s share from 38 percent in 2014 to 27 percent by 2030. That use of a nationwide generation mix as the basis for limits drove the authority dispute. (Printed 969–970.)
sections.Procedural History:
States and private parties petitioned for review when the Clean Power Plan issued. The Supreme Court stayed it in 2016. After an administration change, the D.C. Circuit held litigation in abeyance and later dismissed the original petitions as moot. EPA repealed the plan in 2019 on the ground that § 111 did not authorize generation shifting. Challengers then obtained a D.C. Circuit judgment vacating the repeal because the court regarded EPA’s narrow reading as mistaken. Following another administration change, the court stayed the part of its mandate that would have revived the plan while EPA considered replacement action. (Printed 971.)

Outside procedural supplement: the official opinion, slip opinion pages 13–16 and 31, identifies the petitions for certiorari, resolves the justiciability objection, and reverses and remands the D.C. Circuit judgment. The Court concluded that the states’ injury from the judgment persisted and that the government had not established mootness through voluntary cessation.
sections.Issue: Did § 111(d), through its authorization to identify the best system of emission reduction, authorize emissions caps based on the Clean Power Plan’s system of shifting electricity generation across the national grid? Did that claimed power require clearer authorization because of its novelty, breadth, and economic and political significance? (Printed 972–975.)
sections.Holding: The statute did not authorize the generation-shifting approach used in the Clean Power Plan. The majority treated the claim as a major question requiring clear congressional authorization and found the general word “system,” in this statutory setting, insufficient. The official procedural supplement records reversal and remand. The result concerns this approach to setting the caps; it should not be restated as a holding that all climate regulation or every measure extending beyond an individual plant is unlawful. (Printed 974–975; outside supplement, slip opinion 30–31.)
sections.Reasoning:
Chief Justice Roberts treated agency authority as a contextual statutory question and identified an extraordinary subset of cases in which the history, breadth, and consequences of the claimed power warranted heightened skepticism. Earlier cases involving tobacco, eviction moratoria, greenhouse-gas permitting, assisted suicide, and vaccination requirements illustrated the concern. In that category, textual plausibility alone did not establish delegation; separation-of-powers principles and an understanding of how Congress delegates required clear authorization. (Printed 972–974.)

The plan was extraordinary in the majority’s account because EPA found a transformative power in a rarely used gap-filling provision, departed from its source-focused regulatory history, and adopted an approach Congress had repeatedly declined to enact. The earlier mercury trading rule did not establish the necessary precedent because its cap was based on controls sources could install. The breadth of “system” supplied no sufficiently clear answer to these concerns. (Printed 974–975.)

Justice Kagan, joined by Justices Breyer and Sotomayor, read the broad statutory language as a deliberate grant of flexibility. Generation shifting fit an ordinary understanding of a coordinated system, addressed the pollution that EPA regulates, and operated in a field where EPA had expertise. The dissent understood the precedents as ordinary text-in-context decisions about an agency’s poor fit with a statutory scheme, and contested their conversion into a special clear-statement requirement. It also disputed novelty: every regulation changes generation costs, and the mercury program already used trading to make stricter limits feasible. Broad delegations allow an expert agency to meet important new problems. (Printed 976–980.)

The assigned notes distinguish two supporting rationales. Justice Gorsuch’s concurrence, joined by Justice Alito, linked the doctrine to Article I and nondelegation. Justice Barrett’s later concurrence in Biden v. Nebraska explained it as an ordinary contextual inference about how a principal delegates consequential authority, while expressing concern about strong substantive canons that displace textual meaning. These rationales remain distinct from each other and from the dissent’s objections. (Printed 982–983.)

topics.lrs-i-major-questions: West Virginia requires clear authorization for the extraordinary generation-shifting power at issue.
topics.lrs-i-major-questions-rationales: The majority, Gorsuch, Barrett, and Kagan supply distinct accounts of the doctrine’s legitimacy and operation.
topics.lrs-i-delegated-discretion: The dispute asks how broad statutory language authorizes new agency policy choices and how a court identifies the boundary.
topics.lrs-n-standing-mootness: The Court first rejected the government's argument that the case was moot or that the states lacked standing because EPA had disavowed enforcing the Clean Power Plan.
